title: How many Fed rate cuts in 2026?
description:
This market will resolve according to the exact amount of cuts of 25 basis points in 2026 by the Fed (including any cuts made during the December meeting).

Emergency rate cuts outside of scheduled FOMC meetings will also count toward the total number of cuts in 2026. This market will remain open until December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET, to account for any such emergency actions.

For example, if the Fed cuts rates by 50 bps after a meeting, it would be considered 2 cuts (of 25 bps each).

This market will resolve early to "No" if the specified number of cuts becomes impossible — i.e., if more cuts have already occurred than the strike in question.

Note that cuts between 1–24 bps (inclusive) will also be considered 1 rate cut.

The resolution source for this market will be FOMC statements after meetings scheduled in 2026 according to the official calendar: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm. The level and change of the target federal funds rate is also published at the official website of the Federal Reserve at https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**Persistent inflation above the Fed’s 2% target, combined with a hawkish shift in the June 2026 Summary of Economic Projections, is anchoring trader expectations for zero additional rate cuts in 2026.** The FOMC held the federal funds rate steady at 3.50–3.75% at its July 29 meeting—the fifth consecutive pause—while the June dot plot lifted the median year-end 2026 funds-rate projection to 3.8%, up from 3.4% in March. This revision reflects higher inflation forecasts (core PCE now seen at 3.3% for Q4 2026) and a more resilient labor market, with nine participants projecting at least one hike by year-end.

June CPI data showed headline inflation easing to 3.5% year-over-year from 4.2% in May, aided by falling energy prices after the Iran-related supply shock, yet core readings and the broader trajectory remain elevated enough to keep policy restrictive. With no August FOMC meeting and the next decision in September, markets are awaiting July and August CPI releases plus Chair Warsh’s Jackson Hole remarks (August 27–29) for any signals of easing. The 87.9% market-implied probability of zero cuts captures this consensus for a prolonged hold, while the slim odds of one or more cuts price in only a modest chance that incoming data materially improves the inflation outlook before year-end.
